title: How this guide works
summary: The guide is a set of standalone topic pages you can open in any order, plus an optional journey of practice problems, labs, flashcards and a progress file you can export.
useIf: You want to revise one subject fast, follow the whole journey, or run a group session.
avoidIf: You expect a linear course. Topic pages assume you can jump in and use the related links for depth.

explain.md: This guide teaches AI engineering through **options and trade-offs**, never through one fixed scenario. The main unit is the **topic**: one page you can open from the left menu and revise in about seven minutes. Topics sit inside **chapters** (for example w01 LLM controls and APIs). The sidebar switch **Topics | Journey** chooses between jumping to any topic (the default) and following one question through the stack in order.

steps.title: What it is
steps.md: The mechanism in 150 to 400 words, with a visual.

steps.title: Where and when
steps.md: Concrete places, then use, avoid and flip conditions stated as dials.

steps.title: Alternatives
steps.md: A table with a loses-when column.

steps.title: Scenarios
steps.md: Trade-off cards: choose, then see every verdict.

explain.md: **Practice problems** and **boss rounds** (the Journey mode) turn the same material into game-style levels with dial boards and an interview-style defend task. **Labs** are small interactive tools, seven in total (for example the KV cache sizer and the RRF fusion playground). **Flashcards** use five Leitner boxes and four grades: again, hard, good and easy.

Progress lives in your browser's `localStorage` under the key `ftq.v1`. Export it from the Progress page as `ftq-progress-<name>-<date>.json` and import it later with **merge** (keeps the best of both files, the default) or **replace**. If the browser blocks storage, the guide shows a banner that asks you to export. **Facilitator mode** shows quiz and model answers with an Answer key badge, so keep it off on learners' screens. Press `/` or Ctrl or Cmd K to search.

explain.title: Print a chapter cheat sheet
explain.md: Every chapter has a generated cheat sheet at `#/w/<chapter id>/cheatsheet`. It lists each topic's title, summary, use-if and avoid-if lines, which makes it a fast pre-interview scan.

whereToUse: Before an interview: open the chapter cheat sheet, then drill the topics where your answers feel vague
On a commute or between meetings: one topic, its scenario cards and its flashcards
In a team session: one chapter per session, with the facilitator mode on the host's screen only
After a platform change: re-open the topic and check its dated references, then read the freshness topic
When onboarding a colleague: send the topic links in the order of your stack

use: You know the subject and need to sharpen trade-off reasoning
You have a gap in one chapter and little time
You want evidence of progress that you can share as a file
You coach others and need a structure for a debrief
avoid: You have never heard of the area and need a tutorial first: start with the introductory course in the references, then return
You need a vendor's current price or limit: the guide dates its facts, so confirm in the live documentation
You want to memorise answers: scenario cards change verdicts when a dial moves, so rote answers fail
flips: Time is under 30 minutes: use the cheat sheet and flashcards, skip the practice problems
You study in a group: switch to Journey mode so everyone meets the same boss round
Your browser clears storage: export progress after every session

pitfalls.symptom: Progress vanishes after a browser clean-up
pitfalls.cause: State is stored in `localStorage`, which the browser can clear
pitfalls.fix: Export the JSON file after each session and import it with merge on the new browser

pitfalls.symptom: Learners see answers during a group session
pitfalls.cause: Facilitator mode is a per-browser setting and was left on
pitfalls.fix: Turn it on only on the host's browser and check the Answer key badge before sharing a screen

pitfalls.symptom: A learner reads topics in order and feels lost
pitfalls.cause: Topics are standalone and assume a short refresher, not a lesson sequence
pitfalls.fix: Use the related links at the bottom of each topic, or switch to Journey mode for the story

scenarios.title: Two weeks to an interview
scenarios.situation: A candidate has two weeks. They use the platform daily at work but have never explained their design choices aloud.
constraints: Study time is 30 to 45 minutes a day
The interview is a design conversation, not a coding test
The candidate builds well but explains poorly
unknowns: Is a mock interview partner available?
scenarios.question: How should the candidate use the guide?

options.name: Read every topic once in chapter order
options.why: Complete coverage and a fixed plan.
options.tradeoff: At 7 minutes a topic, 22 topics in one chapter already take more than two hours, so coverage thins out.

options.name: Topic-first on weak chapters, scenario cards daily, boss rounds spoken aloud
options.why: Scenario cards train the trade-off language and boss rounds train the spoken structure, which is the stated weakness.
options.tradeoff: Skipping other chapters leaves blind spots outside the role focus.

options.name: Flashcards only
options.why: Recall of parameter names does not train justification, which is where the candidate is weak.
options.tradeoff: Flashcards are right for the last two days, once the reasoning is in place.

flips.if: The candidate also lacks basic vocabulary
flips.then: Start with the introductory course in the references, then follow the same plan.
Use the cheat sheets for the target chapters and do one boss round aloud.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the mode to the weakness: reasoning needs scenarios, recall needs cards.

scenarios.title: Team workshop on a shared laptop
scenarios.situation: A lead runs a 90 minute session for eight engineers. One laptop is projected. Learners also have the guide open on their own machines.
constraints: Answers must stay hidden until groups commit
unknowns: Do learners use the same browser profile each time?
Is there a printer for cheat sheets?
scenarios.question: How do you set it up?

options.name: Turn facilitator mode on for everyone to speed up review
options.why: Learners see verdicts before they commit, so the trade-off debate never happens.
options.tradeoff: Right for a self-study learner who wants to check an answer after attempting it.

options.name: Let learners read the chapter alone, then discuss
options.tradeoff: Loses the live disagreement that exposes unstated assumptions.

options.name: Facilitator mode on the host laptop only, pairs argue each card, everyone exports progress at the end
options.why: Answers show only where the host controls them, and exported files give each learner a record.
options.tradeoff: The host spends time on the debrief and the export step.

flips.then: Share the host screen with facilitator mode on and have learners vote before each reveal.

flips.if: The group is new to the topic
flips.then: Run Journey mode so they meet the story first.

scenarios.takeaway: Keep answers on the host screen and make learners commit before the reveal.

quiz.q: Where does the guide keep your progress by default?
options: On a server tied to your learner name
In a cookie that expires after 24 hours
In the browser's `localStorage`, exportable as a JSON file
Inside the zip file you opened
quiz.explain: State sits in `localStorage` under `ftq.v1` and can be exported and imported. There is no server, cookies are not used for progress, and the zip is read only.

quiz.q: Which statements about importing a progress file are true?
options: Merge keeps the best of both records
Replace overwrites the current state with the file
quiz.explain: Merge keeps the better record per key and is the default, and replace takes the file as is. Import is a local operation and needs no network.

quiz.q: Put the parts of a topic page in the order you meet them.
items: Where and when to use it
quiz.explain: The page moves from mechanism to decision criteria to comparison to failure, then tests you with scenarios and quick checks.

flashcards.front: What is the main unit of this guide?
flashcards.back: The topic: a standalone page that explains, says where and when to use it, compares alternatives, lists pitfalls and offers scenario cards.

flashcards.front: How do you keep progress across browsers?
flashcards.back: Export the progress JSON from the Progress page and import it elsewhere, using merge to keep the best of both files.
It reveals quiz and model answers with an Answer key badge. Enable it only on the host's screen.
